techniques.name: Causal Discrimination Testing
techniques.description: Causal discrimination testing checks whether a system gives different outputs to otherwise identical inputs because of a protected attribute, by changing only that attribute, or a name, term or other proxy that signals it, and measuring how often or how much the output changes. Galhotra, Brun and Meliou (2017), who called the approach fairness testing, generate inputs from a description of the valid input fields, make copies of each that differ only in the protected attribute (for example, recorded sex), run them all through the system as a black box, and report the causal discrimination score: the share of inputs whose decision changes, sampled until it is known within a chosen margin of error and confidence level. For text, the same test substitutes identity terms or names in otherwise unchanged sentences, such as one religion or ethnicity for another, and reports the average change in the model's score across the substitutions, which Garg et al. (2019) call the counterfactual token fairness gap. Because every other part of the input is held fixed, the test needs no model of how the attribute influences other variables: it measures whether the system itself responds to the attribute, or to the chosen proxy. The output is a score per attribute and, if the tester logs them, the input pairs whose outputs differed.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team tests a credit-approval model before release. For a sample of last year's applications it changes only the applicant's recorded sex, and separately their marital status, re-scores each pair, and reports the share of decisions that flip with a confidence interval, against a release threshold agreed with the compliance function.

A trust-and-safety team checks a toxicity classifier used to hold comments for review by substituting identity terms such as 'gay', 'Muslim' or 'Black' across a set of non-toxic comments. It measures the average change in toxicity score for each term and flags any term whose substitution pushes benign comments over the moderation threshold.

An HR technology supplier tests its CV-ranking service before a client deploys it, by submitting the same CVs under first names and surnames associated with different ethnicities and genders and reporting how often each candidate's rank or shortlisting changes.

A hospital's AI assurance lead tests a symptom-triage assistant with clinical vignettes that differ only in the patient's stated ethnicity. Clinicians first mark which vignettes should be unaffected by ethnicity, and only those pairs count as failures when the urgency rating changes.

limitations.description: Holding every other input fixed measures only the system's direct response to the attribute or proxy. It does not follow through the effects the attribute has on other inputs, such as career breaks on an employment history. Garg et al. note that token substitution is more limited than counterfactual fairness defined on a causal model. Where those downstream effects matter, a clean result does not show that individuals were treated fairly.

The test covers only what is perturbed. Unlisted identity terms, unperturbed proxies and multi-word references go undetected, as does discrimination that appears only when attributes change together: Galhotra et al. measured 11.2% for gender alone but 77.2% for gender, marital status and race together. Garg et al. found mitigation for listed terms generalised much less to held-out terms. A pass covers only the perturbations tried, and the list needs domain review.

Generated inputs may be unrealistic. Themis draws inputs uniformly from the input schema, so the score covers combinations that never occur in practice. Testing real inputs or an existing test suite avoids that, but the score is then only as representative as that set. Galhotra et al. note that Themis computes no confidence level for it, and an interval from a random sample of real cases covers sampling error only.

Not every substitution should leave the output unchanged. Garg et al. give 'That's so gay' versus 'That's so straight' as a pair a toxicity model may rightly score differently, and clinical risk can legitimately depend on sex. Without a judgement about which pairs must match, the test raises false alarms or, if such pairs are excluded wholesale, hides real failures.

A model can pass and still produce very different outcome or error rates across groups, because the test asks only whether changing the attribute changes the output, not whether outcomes are equal. Galhotra et al. distinguish this causal discrimination from group discrimination, and Garg et al. note that a text classifier can satisfy counterfactual fairness while completely failing equality of odds, so it does not replace group metrics.

resources.title: Themis: a software fairness tester (LASER-UMASS/Themis)
resources.abstract: Themis™ is a software fairness tester.

resources.title: Fairness testing: testing software for discrimination
resources.abstract: This paper defines software fairness and discrimination and develops a testing-based method for measuring if and how much software discriminates, focusing on causality in discriminatory behavior. Evidence of software discrimination has been found in modern software systems that recommend criminal sentences, grant access to financial products, and determine who is allowed to participate in promotions. Our approach, Themis, generates efficient test suites to measure discrimination. Given a schema describing valid system inputs, Themis generates discrimination tests automatically and does not require an oracle. We evaluate Themis on 20 software systems, 12 of which come from prior work with explicit focus on avoiding discrimination. We find that (1) Themis is effective at discovering software discrimination, (2) state-of-the-art techniques for removing discrimination from algorithms fail in many situations, at times discriminating against as much as 98% of an input subdomain, (3) Themis optimizations are effective at producing efficient test suites for measuring discrimination, and (4) Themis is more efficient on systems that exhibit more discrimination. We thus demonstrate that fairness testing is a critical aspect of the software development cycle in domains with possible discrimination and provide initial tools for measuring software discrimination.

resources.title: BiasFinder: Metamorphic Test Generation to Uncover Bias for Sentiment Analysis Systems
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems, such as Sentiment Analysis (SA) systems, typically learn from large amounts of data that may reflect human bias. Consequently, such systems may exhibit unintended demographic bias against specific characteristics (e.g., gender, occupation, country-of-origin, etc.). Such bias manifests in an SA system when it predicts different sentiments for similar texts that differ only in the characteristic of individuals described. To automatically uncover bias in SA systems, this paper presents BiasFinder, an approach that can discover biased predictions in SA systems via metamorphic testing. A key feature of BiasFinder is the automatic curation of suitable templates from any given text inputs, using various Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to identify words that describe demographic characteristics. Next, BiasFinder generates new texts from these templates by mutating words associated with a class of a characteristic (e.g., gender-specific words such as female names, she, her). These texts are then used to tease out bias in an SA system. BiasFinder identifies a bias-uncovering test case (BTC) when an SA system predicts different sentiments for texts that differ only in words associated with a different class (e.g., male vs. female) of a target characteristic (e.g., gender). We evaluate BiasFinder on 10 SA systems and 2 large scale datasets, and the results show that BiasFinder can create more BTCs than two popular baselines. We also conduct an annotation study and find that human annotators consistently think that test cases generated by BiasFinder are more fluent than the two baselines.

resources.title: Counterfactual Fairness in Text Classification through Robustness
resources.abstract: In this paper, we study counterfactual fairness in text classification, which asks the question: How would the prediction change if the sensitive attribute referenced in the example were different? Toxicity classifiers demonstrate a counterfactual fairness issue by predicting that "Some people are gay" is toxic while "Some people are straight" is nontoxic. We offer a metric, counterfactual token fairness (CTF), for measuring this particular form of fairness in text classifiers, and describe its relationship with group fairness. Further, we offer three approaches, blindness, counterfactual augmentation, and counterfactual logit pairing (CLP), for optimizing counterfactual token fairness during training, bridging the robustness and fairness literature. Empirically, we find that blindness and CLP address counterfactual token fairness. The methods do not harm classifier performance, and have varying tradeoffs with group fairness. These approaches, both for measurement and optimization, provide a new path forward for addressing fairness concerns in text classification.

resources.title: Gender, Race, and Intersectional Bias in Resume Screening via Language Model Retrieval
resources.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) hiring tools have revolutionized resume screening, and large language models (LLMs) have the potential to do the same. However, given the biases which are embedded within LLMs, it is unclear whether they can be used in this scenario without disadvantaging groups based on their protected attributes. In this work, we investigate the possibilities of using LLMs in a resume screening setting via a document retrieval framework that simulates job candidate selection. Using that framework, we then perform a resume audit study to determine whether a selection of Massive Text Embedding (MTE) models are biased in resume screening scenarios. We simulate this for nine occupations, using a collection of over 500 publicly available resumes and 500 job descriptions. We find that the MTEs are biased, significantly favoring White-associated names in 85.1% of cases and female-associated names in only 11.1% of cases, with a minority of cases showing no statistically significant differences. Further analyses show that Black males are disadvantaged in up to 100% of cases, replicating real-world patterns of bias in employment settings, and validate three hypotheses of intersectionality. We also find an impact of document length as well as the corpus frequency of names in the selection of resumes. These findings have implications for widely used AI tools that are automating employment, fairness, and tech policy.

techniques.name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
techniques.description: A family of data augmentation techniques that generate synthetic minority-class examples through geometric interpolation in feature space, addressing class imbalance problems that degrade classifier performance on underrepresented groups. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), creates new instances by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest neighbours. Extensions include Borderline-SMOTE (focusing generation near decision boundaries), ADASYN (adaptively weighting harder-to-learn instances), and SVMSMOTE (using support vectors to guide generation). These methods operate directly on feature vectors without requiring neural network training, making them computationally lightweight and applicable to any tabular classification task.

example_use_cases.description: Applying SMOTE to oversample underrepresented ethnic groups in a loan approval training dataset, ensuring the classifier has sufficient examples from each demographic group to learn fair decision boundaries.
Using ADASYN to generate synthetic examples of rare manufacturing defect types, improving the reliability of quality control classifiers on edge cases that occur in fewer than 1% of production runs.

Applying Borderline-SMOTE to augment minority-class examples near the decision boundary in a medical diagnosis task, reducing false-negative rates for rare conditions without collecting additional patient data.

Oversampling underrepresented protected groups in a hiring dataset to enable equitable evaluation of candidates across gender and ethnicity, ensuring the model does not simply learn to predict the majority class.

limitations.description: Interpolation in feature space can generate synthetic instances that fall in regions of the feature space not occupied by the true data distribution, introducing noise or unrealistic combinations — particularly problematic for high-dimensional data.
Does not address the root cause of class imbalance (e.g. data collection bias, structural underrepresentation) and may mask rather than resolve underlying fairness issues in the data pipeline.
Performance degrades on high-dimensional datasets where the nearest-neighbour assumption breaks down, and oversampling in such spaces can amplify noise dimensions without improving classification.

Assumes the minority class forms coherent clusters in feature space; when minority examples are scattered or overlap heavily with majority-class regions, interpolation produces ambiguous or mislabelled synthetic samples.

resources.title: SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
resources.abstract: An approach to the construction of classifiers from    imbalanced datasets is described. A dataset is imbalanced if the    classification categories are not approximately equally    represented. Often real-world data sets are predominately composed of    ``normal'' examples with only a small percentage of ``abnormal'' or    ``interesting'' examples. It is also the case that the cost of    misclassifying an abnormal (interesting) example as a normal example    is often much higher than the cost of the reverse    error. Under-sampling of the majority (normal) class has been proposed    as a good means of increasing the sensitivity of a classifier to the    minority class. This paper shows that a combination of our method of    over-sampling the minority (abnormal) class and under-sampling the    majority (normal) class can achieve better classifier performance (in    ROC space) than only under-sampling the majority class.  This paper    also shows that a combination of our method of over-sampling the    minority class and under-sampling the majority class can achieve    better classifier performance (in ROC space) than varying the loss    ratios in Ripper or class priors in Naive Bayes. Our method of    over-sampling the minority class involves creating synthetic minority    class examples.  Experiments are performed using C4.5, Ripper and a    Naive Bayes classifier. The method is evaluated using the area under    the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) and the ROC convex    hull strategy.

resources.title: ADASYN: Adaptive synthetic sampling approach for imbalanced learning
resources.abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive synthetic (ADASYN) sampling approach for learning from imbalanced data sets. The essential idea of ADASYN is to use a weighted distribution for different minority class examples according to their level of difficulty in learning, where more synthetic data is generated for minority class examples that are harder to learn compared to those minority examples that are easier to learn. As a result, the ADASYN approach improves learning with respect to the data distributions in two ways: (1) reducing the bias introduced by the class imbalance, and (2) adaptively shifting the classification decision boundary toward the difficult examples. Simulation analyses on several machine learning data sets show the effectiveness of this method across five evaluation metrics.

resources.title: SMOTE for high-dimensional class-imbalanced data
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Classification using class-imbalanced data is biased in favor of the majority class. The bias is even larger for high-dimensional data, where the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of samples. The problem can be attenuated by undersampling or oversampling, which produce class-balanced data. Generally undersampling is helpful, while random oversampling is not. Synthetic Minority Oversampling TEchnique (SMOTE) is a very popular oversampling method that was proposed to improve random oversampling but its behavior on high-dimensional data has not been thoroughly investigated. In this paper we investigate the properties of SMOTE from a theoretical and empirical point of view, using simulated and real high-dimensional data. RESULTS: While in most cases SMOTE seems beneficial with low-dimensional data, it does not attenuate the bias towards the classification in the majority class for most classifiers when data are high-dimensional, and it is less effective than random undersampling. SMOTE is beneficial for k-NN classifiers for high-dimensional data if the number of variables is reduced performing some type of variable selection; we explain why, otherwise, the k-NN classification is biased towards the minority class. Furthermore, we show that on high-dimensional data SMOTE does not change the class-specific mean values while it decreases the data variability and it introduces correlation between samples. We explain how our findings impact the class-prediction for high-dimensional data. CONCLUSIONS: In practice, in the high-dimensional setting only k-NN classifiers based on the Euclidean distance seem to benefit substantially from the use of SMOTE, provided that variable selection is performed before using SMOTE; the benefit is larger if more neighbors are used. SMOTE for k-NN without variable selection should not be used, because it strongly biases the classification towards the minority class.

resources.title: A Comparison of Undersampling, Oversampling, and SMOTE Methods for Dealing with Imbalanced Classification in Educational Data Mining
resources.abstract: Educational data mining is capable of producing useful data-driven applications (e.g., early warning systems in schools or the prediction of students’ academic achievement) based on predictive models. However, the class imbalance problem in educational datasets could hamper the accuracy of predictive models as many of these models are designed on the assumption that the predicted class is balanced. Although previous studies proposed several methods to deal with the imbalanced class problem, most of them focused on the technical details of how to improve each technique, while only a few focused on the application aspect, especially for the application of data with different imbalance ratios. In this study, we compared several sampling techniques to handle the different ratios of the class imbalance problem (i.e., moderately or extremely imbalanced classifications) using the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 dataset. For our comparison, we used random oversampling (ROS), random undersampling (RUS), and the combination of the synthetic minority oversampling technique for nominal and continuous (SMOTE-NC) and RUS as a hybrid resampling technique. We used the Random Forest as our classification algorithm to evaluate the results of each sampling technique. Our results show that random oversampling for moderately imbalanced data and hybrid resampling for extremely imbalanced data seem to work best. The implications for educational data mining applications and suggestions for future research are discussed.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

resources.title: Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

resources.title: Using quantile regression to extend an existing wind power forecasting system with probabilistic forecasts
resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

sample_claims.text: The flood forecasting model estimates the specified lower and upper conditional quantiles of river level without imposing a symmetric error distribution, and how often observed levels fall inside them has been checked on held-out events.

The 90th percentile recovery-time forecast exceeds the observed recovery time for at least 90% of patients in the held-out audit sample, so the quoted longest timeframe is not systematically too short.
The wind power forecast's 10th to 90th percentile band contains observed output about 80% of the time on out-of-sample data, in each of the low, medium and high wind-speed ranges.

techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

resources.title: Assessing calibration and bias of a deployed machine learning malnutrition prediction model within a large healthcare system
resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

Uncertainty-aware body composition analysis with deep regression ensembles on UK Biobank MRI
resources.abstract: Along with rich health-related metadata, medical images have been acquired for over 40,000 male and female UK Biobank participants, aged 44-82, since 2014. Phenotypes derived from these images, such as measurements of body composition from MRI, can reveal new links between genetics, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic conditions. In this work, six measurements of body composition and adipose tissues were automatically estimated by image-based, deep regression with ResNet50 neural networks from neck-to-knee body MRI. Despite the potential for high speed and accuracy, these networks produce no output segmentations that could indicate the reliability of individual measurements. The presented experiments therefore examine uncertainty quantification with mean-variance regression and ensembling to estimate individual measurement errors and thereby identify potential outliers, anomalies, and other failure cases automatically. In 10-fold cross-validation on data of about 8500 subjects, mean-variance regression and ensembling showed complementary benefits, reducing the mean absolute error across all predictions by 12%. Both improved the calibration of uncertainties and their ability to identify high prediction errors. With intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) above 0.97, all targets except the liver fat content yielded relative measurement errors below 5%. Testing on another 1000 subjects showed consistent performance, and the method was finally deployed for inference to 30,000 subjects with missing reference values. The results indicate that deep regression ensembles could ultimately provide automated, uncertainty-aware measurements of body composition for more than 120,000 UK Biobank neck-to-knee body MRI that are to be acquired within the coming years.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Ensembles
techniques.description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

example_use_cases.description: An electricity network operator forecasting next-day demand at each substation trains 100 gradient-boosted models on bootstrap replicates of three years of meter readings, resampled in whole-week blocks because consecutive readings are correlated. Planners hold extra reserve at substations where the models' forecasts spread widely, because those are the sites whose forecasts the historical data settle least.

A hospital's readmission-risk tool shows clinicians, beside each patient's predicted risk, the range of risks given by models trained on bootstrap replicates of the training cohort, resampling patients rather than admissions so that one patient's admissions stay together, so that a clinician can see when an estimate rests on few comparable past patients and give it less weight in discharge planning.

A local authority reviewing a housing-need scoring model compares the average spread of bootstrap-ensemble scores across applicant groups and finds it widest for a group with few past applications, which shows that the model's scores for that group are least settled by the data; it collects more cases before letting the scores inform priority for that group.

limitations.description: Every member of the ensemble is a full training run, and every prediction must be made by every member, so training cost, storage and prediction time all grow in proportion to the number of replicates. For large neural networks this usually limits the ensemble to a handful of members, too few for stable percentiles of the spread.

The spread measures uncertainty in the fitted model, not the noise in outcomes. Presented as the range within which a case's actual outcome will fall, it understates the uncertainty, most of all where outcomes are noisy and training data plentiful, so the outcome noise has to be estimated separately, for example from held-out errors, and added.

The spread reflects only what the procedure lets vary: which cases are in each training set and, for models trained from a random start such as neural networks, each member's starting point. Fixed choices such as features, architecture and training settings add no spread. A model consistently wrong for a group the data under-represent can show little spread there, and members can agree closely on inputs unlike the training data, so a small spread is not evidence of reliability.

Each replicate contains on average only about 63 per cent of the distinct training cases, so each member learns from less information than a model trained on all the data. With small datasets or rare classes, some replicates may contain almost none of a rare class or subgroup, which inflates the spread for those cases and can leave individual members unusable.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. With repeated measurements of the same person, time series or other grouped data, case resampling spreads related cases across replicates and understates the uncertainty, unless whole groups or time blocks are resampled instead.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

techniques.name: Jackknife Resampling
techniques.description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data team fits a readmission-risk model on 600 patient records and refits it 600 times, leaving out one patient each time. The spread of the refitted coefficients shows which risk factors are stable enough to report, and the records whose removal shifts the fit most go back to clinicians to check for entry errors.

A water utility's analysts estimate how rainfall drives reservoir inflow from 40 annual observations. Leaving out each year in turn gives a variance estimate for the fitted slope and shows whether a single flood year drives the result, before the figure goes into a planning document.

A credit-risk team documents its scorecard's stability for model validators by refitting it with each of 800 sampled loan records left out. It reports the records whose removal changes any coefficient by more than a stated tolerance, so validators can see how much of the model rests on a few loans.

limitations.description: Computationally heavy when the result needs a model refit, since n records mean n refits, which is impractical for datasets with thousands or millions of records or for costly training. Simple statistics that are cheap to recompute do not have this problem.

Works only for statistics that change smoothly when one record is removed. For quantities that jump, such as the number of clusters in a mixture model, leave-one-out estimates are unreliable. Even for smooth statistics the variance estimate tends to run high, so intervals are conservative.

Assumes the records are independent. With repeated or clustered measurements, such as several visits per patient or neighbouring regions, leaving out one record leaves its close relatives in the data, so the refits barely change and the spread understates the true uncertainty.
Provides limited insight into model behaviour on truly novel data, as each jackknife sample is only minimally different from the full training set.

Measures how sensitive a result is to the sample in hand, not whether the model is right. A stable fit can still be systematically wrong, so a narrow spread across refits is no evidence of accuracy, or of performance on a different population.

techniques.name: Cross-validation
techniques.description: Cross-validation estimates how well a model will perform on data it has not seen, and how much that estimate depends on the particular data used. The dataset is divided into k parts called folds, the model is trained on all but one fold and scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats until every fold has served as the held-out set once. The scores are averaged to give a performance estimate, and their spread gives a rough indication of how much the result depends on which data the model was trained on. Common variants are stratified cross-validation, where each fold keeps the overall class proportions, and leave-one-out, where each fold is a single example. A large gap between training scores and held-out scores points to overfitting, where a model has learned quirks of its training data that do not carry over to new data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data-science team has records for about 900 patients and is building a readmission-risk model. It runs 10-fold cross-validation with each patient's admissions kept in the same fold, then reports the mean and spread of held-out scores. A wide spread, or a large gap to the training score, tells the team the model is not yet stable enough to take to a prospective trial.

A bank's fraud team compares three candidate classifiers by running the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation on a year of labelled transactions, so every candidate is scored on identical folds and the rare fraud cases are spread evenly across them. They select the model with the best mean recall at a fixed false-alarm rate and drop any candidate whose fold-to-fold scores vary widely.

A materials-science group has only 120 labelled samples from costly experiments. Instead of trusting one train-test split, it repeats 5-fold cross-validation with different random splits and reports the spread of the accuracy estimate, which decides whether the model is reliable enough to guide the next round of experiments.

limitations.description: The number of folds trades cost against bias and variance. Each fold is another training run. Few folds (2 to 5) train on less data and tend to understate performance, whereas leave-one-out has little bias but unstable estimates and the highest cost. Ten folds is a common compromise, not a rule.

Assumes records are independent. If the same patient, customer or site appears in several records, a fold can be trained on records nearly identical to those it is tested on, and the score is optimistic. Folds must then be built by group, not drawn at random.

Ignores time order. Training on later records and testing on earlier ones lets future information leak into the estimate and flatters the model. For time-ordered data, use an evaluation that always tests on data later than the training data, such as rolling-origin evaluation.

Anything learned from the data must be fitted inside each training fold, including scaling, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Done once on the full dataset beforehand, it leaks test-fold information and inflates the scores. Tuning and reporting on the same folds is also optimistic, so nested cross-validation is needed for both.

A score from a small sample is imprecise, and the spread across folds understates the true uncertainty. In one neuroimaging study, error bars on a cross-validated score were roughly plus or minus 10% with 100 samples, so a small gain between two models can be noise.

resources.title: Cross-validation failure: Small sample sizes lead to large error bars
resources.abstract: Predictive models ground many state‐of‐the‐art developments in statistical brain image analysis: decoding, MVPA, searchlight, or extraction of biomarkers. The principled approach to establish their validity and usefulness is cross‐validation, testing prediction on unseen data. Here, I would like to raise awareness on error bars of cross‐validation, which are often underestimated. Simple experiments show that sample sizes of many neuroimaging studies inherently lead to large error bars, eg Symbol for 100 samples. The standard error across folds strongly underestimates them. These large error bars compromise the reliability of conclusions drawn with predictive models, such as biomarkers or methods developments where, unlike with cognitive neuroimaging MVPA approaches, more samples cannot be acquired by repeating the experiment across many subjects. Solutions to increase sample size must be investigated, tackling possible increases in heterogeneity of the data.

techniques.name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
techniques.description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. Neither precision nor recall uses true negatives, so a large majority class does not flatter the score as it can flatter accuracy and AUC-ROC. A model with no skill scores about the proportion of positives in the data, so the score is only meaningful next to that baseline.

example_use_cases.description: A payments team compares candidate fraud models on a held-out month of transactions in which about 1 in 500 is fraudulent. It ranks them by AUPRC against the 0.2% no-skill baseline, then reads the best model's curve to choose a threshold that keeps false alarms within what the investigation team can review.

A hospital evaluates a model that screens for a rare condition affecting about 1 in 200 patients. ROC AUC can look high even when most flagged patients are healthy, so the team reports AUPRC against the 0.5% baseline and reads the precision at the recall clinicians require, to decide whether the follow-up workload is manageable.

A manufacturer compares two defect-detection models for a production line where about 1 in 1,000 parts is faulty. It uses AUPRC on a labelled validation batch to choose between them, so that a model is not preferred simply for labelling nearly every good part correctly.

limitations.description: AUPRC depends on the share of positives in the data, so scores from datasets or groups with different proportions cannot be compared directly, and no universal pass mark can be set. Each score has to be read against its own no-skill baseline, which is about the positive proportion.

It treats one class as the positive class and ignores true negatives, so it says nothing about how reliably the model clears the majority class. That matters where certifying a case as negative or safe is as important as catching positives.

A single area averages over every threshold, including ones no deployment would use, and can hide poor precision at the recall the application needs. Choosing the operating point needs a look at that part of the curve and the cost of each kind of error.

The area can be computed in different ways. Trapezoidal linear interpolation between points gives an overly optimistic value, whereas step-wise average precision does not, so scores from different libraries or settings may not match.
Few positive test cases make precision-recall estimates unstable, so a high score from a small sample may not hold on a larger, representative evaluation set.

resources.title: The relationship between Precision-Recall and ROC curves
resources.abstract: Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curves are commonly used to present results for binary decision problems in machine learning. However, when dealing with highly skewed datasets, Precision-Recall (PR) curves give a more informative picture of an algorithm's performance. We show that a deep connection exists between ROC space and PR space, such that a curve dominates in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space. A corollary is the notion of an achievable PR curve, which has properties much like the convex hull in ROC space; we show an efficient algorithm for computing this curve. Finally, we also note differences in the two types of curves are significant for algorithm design. For example, in PR space it is incorrect to linearly interpolate between points. Furthermore, algorithms that optimize the area under the ROC curve are not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve.

Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

techniques.name: Reweighing
techniques.description: Reweighing is a pre-processing method, from Kamiran and Calders (2012), that removes the statistical association between a protected attribute and the outcome label in training data by giving each training example a weight, without changing any feature values or labels. For every combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired), the weight is the number of examples that combination would have if group and label were independent, divided by the number it actually has: the group's share of the data times the label's share, over the combination's observed share. Combinations rarer than independence predicts, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so that in the weighted data every group has the same rate of positive labels. A model is then trained on the original data using these weights; the outputs are the weighted training set and a small table of weights that records exactly how each group-label combination was adjusted.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

An auditor reviewing a benefits-fraud model asks for the table of reweighing weights kept with the training run. A weight of 1.8 on one nationality group's not-fraud cases shows how far that group's historical labels departed from independence, and the table records exactly how the training data were adjusted, so the auditor can reconstruct the intervention without rerunning it.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity). It does not aim at equal error rates such as equal opportunity, and the weights are computed once, before training, so they cannot respond to where the trained model actually errs. An adaptive variant (Krasanakis et al., 2018) re-estimates weights during training for error-rate criteria, but it has no maintained implementation.

It removes all association between group and label, including any part a legitimate factor explains. Kamiran and Calders give the example of car insurance, where more accidents among men may justify different outcomes by sex; reweighing erases that difference too, so it over-corrects wherever some gap between groups is warranted.

The learning algorithm must accept example weights; where it cannot, the data have to be resampled instead, which is a different method. Only the training data are balanced, so the trained model's predictions are not guaranteed to be: outcome rates by group must be measured on held-out data after training rather than assumed.

When a group-label combination is rare its weight is large (a combination with a tenth of its expected count gets a weight of ten), so a handful of examples can dominate training. This raises variance and amplifies any labelling errors in exactly the group the method is meant to protect, and it bites hardest with small or intersectional groups.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

resources.title: Bias Discovery in Machine Learning Models for Mental Health
resources.abstract: Fairness and bias are crucial concepts in artificial intelligence, yet they are relatively ignored in machine learning applications in clinical psychiatry. We computed fairness metrics and present bias mitigation strategies using a model trained on clinical mental health data. We collected structured data related to the admission, diagnosis, and treatment of patients in the psychiatry department of the University Medical Center Utrecht. We trained a machine learning model to predict future administrations of benzodiazepines on the basis of past data. We found that gender plays an unexpected role in the predictions—this constitutes bias. Using the AI Fairness 360 package, we implemented reweighing and discrimination-aware regularization as bias mitigation strategies, and we explored their implications for model performance. This is the first application of bias exploration and mitigation in a machine learning model trained on real clinical psychiatry data.

The method modifies non-protected features through mathematical transformations that preserve the utility of the data whilst reducing correlations that could lead to discriminatory outcomes. This approach specifically targets the '80% rule' disparate impact threshold by adjusting feature distributions to ensure more equitable treatment across demographic groups in downstream model predictions.

resources.title: Certifying and Removing Disparate Impact
resources.abstract: What does it mean for an algorithm to be biased? In U.S. law, unintentional bias is encoded via disparate impact, which occurs when a selection process has widely different outcomes for different groups, even as it appears to be neutral. This legal determination hinges on a definition of a protected class (ethnicity, gender) and an explicit description of the process. When computers are involved, determining disparate impact (and hence bias) is harder. It might not be possible to disclose the process. In addition, even if the process is open, it might be hard to elucidate in a legal setting how the algorithm makes its decisions. Instead of requiring access to the process, we propose making inferences based on the data it uses. We present four contributions. First, we link disparate impact to a measure of classification accuracy that while known, has received relatively little attention. Second, we propose a test for disparate impact based on how well the protected class can be predicted from the other attributes. Third, we describe methods by which data might be made unbiased. Finally, we present empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of our test for disparate impact and our approach for both masking bias and preserving relevant information in the data. Interestingly, our approach resembles some actual selection practices that have recently received legal scrutiny.
