techniques.name: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness Assessment
techniques.description: A causal fairness evaluation technique that assesses algorithmic discrimination by examining specific causal pathways in a model's decision-making process. Unlike general counterfactual fairness, this approach enables practitioners to identify and intervene on particular causal paths that may introduce bias whilst preserving other legitimate pathways. The method uses causal graphs to distinguish between direct discrimination (through protected attributes) and indirect discrimination (through seemingly neutral factors that correlate with protected attributes), allowing for more nuanced fairness assessments in complex causal settings.

example_use_cases.description: Evaluating hiring algorithms by identifying which causal pathways from education and experience legitimately affect job performance versus those that introduce gender or racial bias, enabling targeted interventions that preserve merit-based selection whilst eliminating discriminatory pathways.

Analysing loan approval models to provide transparent evidence of which factors legitimately influence creditworthiness versus those that create indirect discrimination, enabling clear explanations to regulators about causal mechanisms underlying fair lending decisions.

limitations.description: Requires identifying which causal pathways are 'allowable' and which are not—a subjective decision; analyzing specific paths adds complexity to the causal model and the fairness criterion.

Causal graph construction relies on domain expertise and cannot be validated from observational data alone; if the graph incorrectly encodes causal structure or omits relevant edges, the path-specific assessment may certify an unfair model as compliant with no internal mechanism to detect the error, and this uncertainty is rarely surfaced in compliance documentation.

Path-specific causal effects are frequently non-identifiable from observational data alone; when unobserved confounders exist between a sensitive attribute and mediating variables or outcomes, the effect along a specific pathway cannot be uniquely recovered without additional parametric assumptions, reducing the technique to bounding rather than point-estimation of discrimination.

resources.title: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of learning fair decision systems from data in which a sensitive attribute might affect the decision along both fair and unfair pathways. We introduce a counterfactual approach to disregard effects along unfair pathways that does not incur in the same loss of individual-specific information as previous approaches. Our method corrects observations adversely affected by the sensitive attribute, and uses these to form a decision. We leverage recent developments in deep learning and approximate inference to develop a VAE-type method that is widely applicable to complex nonlinear models.

resources.title: A Causal Framework for Discovering and Removing Direct and Indirect Discrimination
resources.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the problem of discovering both direct and indirect discrimination from the historical data, and removing the discriminatory effects before the data is used for predictive analysis (e.g., building classifiers). The main drawback of existing methods is that they cannot distinguish the part of influence that is really caused by discrimination from all correlated influences. In our approach, we make use of the causal network to capture the causal structure of the data. Then we model direct and indirect discrimination as the path-specific effects, which accurately identify the two types of discrimination as the causal effects transmitted along different paths in the network. Based on that, we propose an effective algorithm for discovering direct and indirect discrimination, as well as an algorithm for precisely removing both types of discrimination while retaining good data utility. Experiments using the real dataset show the effectiveness of our approaches.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis: A Causal Toolkit for Fair Machine Learning
resources.abstract: Decision-making systems based on AI and machine learning have been used throughout a wide range of real-world scenarios, including healthcare, law enforcement, education, and finance. It is no longer far-fetched to envision a future where autonomous systems will drive entire business decisions and, more broadly, support large-scale decision-making infrastructure to solve society’s most challenging problems. Issues of unfairness and discrimination are pervasive when decisions are being made by humans, and remain (or are potentially amplified) when decisions are made using machines with little transparency, accountability, and fairness. In this monograph, we introduce a framework for causal fairness analysis with the intent of filling in this gap, i.e., understanding, modeling, and possibly solving issues of fairness in decision-making settings. The main insight of our approach will be to link the quantification of the disparities present in the observed data with the underlying, often unobserved, collection of causal mechanisms that generate the disparity in the first place, a challenge we call the Fundamental Problem of Causal Fairness Analysis (FPCFA). In order to solve the FPCFA, we study the problem of decomposing variations and empirical measures of fairness that attribute such variations to structural mechanisms and different units of the population. Our effort culminates in the Fairness Map, the first systematic attempt to organize and explain the relationship between various criteria found in the literature. Finally, we study which causal assumptions are minimally needed for performing causal fairness analysis and propose the Fairness Cookbook, which allows one to assess the existence of disparate impact and disparate treatment.

resources.title: Causal Fairness Analysis vignette: Census bias detection
Path-specific effects for pulse-oximetry guided decisions in critical care
resources.abstract: Identifying and measuring biases associated with sensitive attributes is a crucial consideration in healthcare to prevent treatment disparities. One prominent issue is inaccurate pulse oximeter readings, which tend to overestimate oxygen saturation for dark-skinned patients and misrepresent supplemental oxygen needs. Most existing research has revealed statistical disparities linking device measurement errors to patient outcomes in intensive care units (ICUs) without causal formalization. This study causally investigates how racial discrepancies in oximetry measurements affect invasive ventilation in ICU settings. We employ a causal inference-based approach using path-specific effects to isolate the impact of bias by race on clinical decision-making. To estimate these effects, we leverage a doubly robust estimator, propose its self-normalized variant for improved sample efficiency, and provide novel finite-sample guarantees. Our methodology is validated on semi-synthetic data and applied to two large real-world health datasets: MIMIC-IV and eICU. Contrary to prior work, our analysis reveals minimal impact of racial discrepancies on invasive ventilation rates. However, path-specific effects mediated by oxygen saturation disparity are more pronounced on ventilation duration, and the severity differs across datasets. Our work provides a novel pipeline for investigating potential disparities in clinical decision-making and, more importantly, highlights the necessity of causal methods to robustly assess fairness in healthcare.

techniques.name: Fair Bayesian Optimisation
techniques.description: Fair Bayesian Optimisation (FairBO) tunes a model's hyperparameters, the settings fixed before training such as tree depth or regularisation strength, to find the most accurate model that also meets a fairness threshold chosen in advance, for example a difference in positive-prediction rates between two groups of at most 0.05. Because it only changes hyperparameters and retrains, it treats the model and its training pipeline as a black box, so it works with any model class and any group fairness metric, can enforce several metrics at once, and returns a model that need not use the protected attribute at prediction time (the attribute is still needed to measure fairness during the search). Each step trains a model with a candidate configuration and measures its validation accuracy and fairness, and two Gaussian processes (statistical models that predict a value together with its uncertainty) are fitted to the results of the configurations tried so far. The next configuration is the one with the highest expected improvement in accuracy weighted by the predicted probability of meeting the fairness constraint; until a fair configuration has been found, the search maximises that probability alone. The output is the best configuration that met the constraint, with its accuracy and fairness measurements.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team tunes a gradient-boosted credit-risk model under a constraint that the approval-rate difference between applicants of different nationality stays at or below 0.05. It records the most accurate configuration that met the constraint beside the result of unconstrained tuning, so the model approval committee can see what accuracy the constraint cost.

An HR analytics team at a large employer tunes a random forest that ranks job applications for interview, enforcing limits on the gender gap in true positive rates and on the gap in shortlisting rates at the same time, because its policy commits to both equal opportunity and comparable shortlisting rates.

A data science team at a health insurer already runs an adversarially debiased claims-triage model whose fairness changed sharply with its learning rate and adversary weight. It uses FairBO to tune those hyperparameters under a statistical parity constraint, rather than tuning them for accuracy alone and checking fairness afterwards.

A local authority building a model to prioritise benefit-fraud reviews cannot use ethnicity as an input at decision time. It holds ethnicity only in a validation extract, uses FairBO to select hyperparameters that keep the referral-rate gap within its equality impact assessment threshold, and then confirms the gap on a separate held-out sample before deployment.

limitations.description: It can only reach fairness that some hyperparameter setting already provides. If no configuration in the search space meets the threshold, it returns no fair model. The originating paper found that regularisation hyperparameters (tree depth, weight penalties, learning rate) have the largest effect on fairness, so a search space without them leaves fewer fair options.

The fairness metric and its threshold must be fixed before the search, and the result says nothing about metrics that were not constrained. Choosing them is a normative decision the method does not make. If decision-makers need to see the whole accuracy-fairness trade-off before picking a threshold, a multi-objective search is needed, which the paper found slower to reach a model meeting a given threshold.

A constraint can be met by a model that barely distinguishes between anyone. The paper argues that as regularisation grows, predictions approach a constant and satisfy every group fairness metric, and in its example run on the Adult dataset (random forest, parity gap at most 0.05) random search found fair models only at the accuracy of always predicting the majority class. Check accuracy and error rates within each group, not only the fairness gap, before accepting the result.

Every step trains a full model, so the cost is the training cost multiplied by the number of evaluations (the paper used up to 100), which is expensive for large models. The fairness value guiding the search is estimated on the validation split used during tuning, so it carries sampling error that is large when a group is small; confirm the gap on held-out data before relying on it.

It has little evidence behind it and no maintained implementation. The paper tests only binary classification with a binary protected attribute on three tabular datasets, leaving regression, image and language tasks to future work. The code shipped in AutoGluon 0.3.1 (2021) and was dropped in 0.4.0; Syne Tune moved it to a legacy folder in 0.14 and removed it in 0.15 (December 2025), though its documentation still describes it. Use means pinning an old release or rebuilding it.

resources.title: Fair Bayesian Optimization
resources.abstract: Given the increasing importance of machine learning (ML) in our lives, several algorithmic fairness techniques have been proposed to mitigate biases in the outcomes of the ML models. However, most of these techniques are specialized to cater to a single family of ML models and a specific definition of fairness, limiting their adaptibility in practice. We introduce a general constrained Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to optimize the performance of any ML model while enforcing one or multiple fairness constraints. BO is a model-agnostic optimization method that has been successfully applied to automatically tune the hyperparameters of ML models. We apply BO with fairness constraints to a range of popular models, including random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, showing that we can obtain accurate and fair solutions by acting solely on the hyperparameters. We also show empirically that our approach is competitive with specialized techniques that enforce model-specific fairness constraints, and outperforms preprocessing methods that learn fair representations of the input data. Moreover, our method can be used in synergy with such specialized fairness techniques to tune their hyperparameters. Finally, we study the relationship between fairness and the hyperparameters selected by BO. We observe a correlation between regularization and unbiased models, explaining why acting on the hyperparameters leads to ML models that generalize well and are fair.

techniques.name: Constitutional AI Evaluation
techniques.description: Constitutional AI evaluation checks whether a language model follows the written principles, or 'constitution', that it was trained or instructed to follow. The evaluator writes test prompts for each principle, and can add prompts where two principles conflict or where a user tries to talk the model out of a principle. A judge, either human reviewers or a second language model whose accuracy has been checked, assesses each response against one principle at a time, often by comparing it with a baseline model's response. The result is a rate for each principle, such as how often the model's response is preferred to the baseline's, which shows which principles it follows well on the prompts tested and which it does not. A fuller evaluation also checks that following the principles has not made the model over-cautious or less capable.

example_use_cases.description: A developer tuning a general-purpose assistant on a constitution that includes 'refuse requests for illegal activity' writes test prompts for each principle, including borderline chemistry-education questions and attempts to extract synthesis instructions. Reviewers compare the tuned model's answers with the base model's, to decide whether the constitution is ready to ship or needs principles rewritten.

A news publisher using an AI summariser governed by a neutrality principle gives it the same contested story framed from several political positions. Reviewers from differing viewpoints score whether each summary adds editorial language, and the editors use the rate by topic to decide where the summariser can run without a human check.

A digital health provider tests a mental health support chatbot built on the principle 'be supportive, but never diagnose' with scripted crisis conversations in which users ask directly for a diagnosis. Clinicians score each reply, and the share that stays on the right side of the boundary decides whether the chatbot is cleared for a limited pilot.

An education company checks a homework assistant built on the principle 'guide learning without giving direct answers' across subjects, age bands and frustrated or urgent requests. It counts replies that simply give the answer, and uses the rate for each subject to decide where the principle needs strengthening before a school rollout.

limitations.description: Principles are written in natural language, so compliance depends on how the judge reads them. Vague principles, or ones that mean different things across cultures and languages, give scores that reviewers would dispute, so the judge's reading needs checking against human reviewers for each principle.

Principles can conflict in complex scenarios, and the evaluation has to decide which should win. If the intended priority is not written down, a model can look compliant on each principle separately and still resolve conflicts differently from what the developer intended.

Adherence is uneven across kinds of principle. In one study of small fine-tuned models, negatively framed principles such as avoiding harmful content were followed much better than positively framed, abstract ones such as benefiting humanity, so an average score can hide principles the model largely ignores.

Scores depend on the test prompts and on the judge. Prompts that miss a principle's edge cases give a falsely high rate, and an automated judge can favour one response position or misapply the principle, so it needs checking against human judgement in each new domain.

When principles are revised after deployment, results must be re-run, and comparing them across principle versions is hard because a change in score may come from the model, the principles or the test criteria.

resources.title: C3AI: Crafting and Evaluating Constitutions for Constitutional AI
resources.abstract: Constitutional AI (CAI) guides LLM behavior using constitutions, but identifying which principles are most effective for model alignment remains an open challenge. We introduce the C3AI framework (Crafting Constitutions for CAI models), which serves two key functions: (1) selecting and structuring principles to form effective constitutions before fine-tuning; and (2) evaluating whether fine-tuned CAI models follow these principles in practice. By analyzing principles from AI and psychology, we found that positively framed, behavior-based principles align more closely with human preferences than negatively framed or trait-based principles. In a safety alignment use case, we applied a graph-based principle selection method to refine an existing CAI constitution, improving safety measures while maintaining strong general reasoning capabilities. Interestingly, fine-tuned CAI models performed well on negatively framed principles but struggled with positively framed ones, in contrast to our human alignment results. This highlights a potential gap between principle design and model adherence. Overall, C3AI provides a structured and scalable approach to both crafting and evaluating CAI constitutions.

resources.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
resources.abstract: As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs. We experiment with methods for training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement, without any human labels identifying harmful outputs. The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'. The process involves both a supervised learning and a reinforcement learning phase. In the supervised phase we sample from an initial model, then generate self-critiques and revisions, and then finetune the original model on revised responses. In the RL phase, we sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences. We then train with RL using the preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF). As a result we are able to train a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them. Both the SL and RL methods can leverage chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve the human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. These methods make it possible to control AI behavior more precisely and with far fewer human labels.

resources.title: Domain-Specific Constitutional AI: Enhancing Safety in LLM-Powered Mental Health Chatbots
resources.abstract: Mental health applications have emerged as a critical area in computational health, driven by rising global rates of mental illness, the integration of AI in psychological care, and the need for scalable solutions in underserved communities. These include therapy chatbots, crisis detection, and wellness platforms handling sensitive data, requiring specialized AI safety beyond general safeguards due to emotional vulnerability, risks like misdiagnosis or symptom exacerbation, and precise management of vulnerable states to avoid severe outcomes such as self-harm or loss of trust. Despite AI safety advances, general safeguards inadequately address mental health-specific challenges, including crisis intervention accuracy to avert escalations, therapeutic guideline adherence to prevent misinformation, scale limitations in resource-constrained settings, and adaptation to nuanced dialogues where generics may introduce biases or miss distress signals. We introduce an approach to apply Constitutional AI training with domain-specific mental health principles for safe, domain-adapted CAI systems in computational mental health applications.

resources.title: Collective Constitutional AI: Aligning a Language Model with Public Input
resources.abstract: There is growing consensus that language model (LM) developers should not be the sole deciders of LM behavior, creating a need for methods that enable the broader public to collectively shape the behavior of LM systems that affect them. To address this need, we present Collective Constitutional AI (CCAI): a multi-stage process for sourcing and integrating public input into LMs—from identifying a target population to sourcing principles to training and evaluating a model. We demonstrate the real-world practicality of this approach by creating what is, to our knowledge, the first LM fine-tuned with collectively sourced public input and evaluating this model against a baseline model trained with established principles from a LM developer. Our quantitative evaluations demonstrate several benefits of our approach: the CCAI-trained model shows lower bias across nine social dimensions compared to the baseline model, while maintaining equivalent performance on language, math, and helpful-harmless evaluations. Qualitative comparisons of the models suggest that the models differ on the basis of their respective constitutions, e.g., when prompted with contentious topics, the CCAI-trained model tends to generate responses that reframe the matter positively instead of a refusal. These results demonstrate a promising, tractable pathway toward publicly informed development of language models.

techniques.name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
techniques.description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input an arbitrary label unrelated to its content, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company that licenses a chest X-ray classifier for installation on hospital servers, where the weights leave its control, embeds a trigger set before each release and lodges the commitments with a timestamping service. When a near-identical model appears in a rival's product, it queries that product with the trigger images to decide whether there is enough evidence to pursue a licence breach.

Before relying on the watermark in its licence terms, the security team of a retailer that licenses a visual product-search model to partner stores to run on their own servers runs the fine-tuning and pruning attacks in its threat model against the watermarked model, and reports the trigger-set accuracy that survives each, to set the verification threshold and state what the watermark can and cannot evidence.

In a licensing dispute over a satellite-imagery land-use classifier used by a local authority, the developer opens its pre-release commitments to an independent expert, who queries the disputed model's prediction service with the trigger images and reports the match rate against a threshold agreed in advance, without either party handing over model weights.

limitations.description: Removal attacks defeat it in practice. A systematic evaluation of published schemes, trigger-set schemes among them, found none robust against adaptive removal attacks or known ways of deriving a surrogate model, and in the originating paper re-training all layers sharply reduced trigger-set accuracy in models watermarked by fine-tuning. A failed verification does not show a model was not copied, and a robustness claim holds only for the attacks tested.

It evidences copying of the model, not theft through its prediction interface, and needs query access to the suspect. A copy trained on the deployed model's answers (model extraction or distillation) need never see the trigger inputs, and a systematic evaluation found these schemes fail against such surrogates, so extraction needs other defences. A copy used only inside its owner's organisation, or not exposed to queries, cannot be tested at all.

Verification reveals the secret. Sending trigger inputs to a suspect's interface, or showing them to an arbiter, exposes them; an adversary who learns them can fine-tune them away or filter those queries, so verification is in effect single-use unless several trigger sets were embedded or a zero-knowledge protocol is used, both of which the originating paper describes and both of which add work.

Without commitments lodged before release the evidence is weak: whoever holds a copy can embed a second trigger set of their own and claim ownership. In the originating paper's experiments the second set was much less durable under fine-tuning than the first, but that helps only an owner who can show its commitments existed before the disputed model did.

The scheme and its evaluations cover image classifiers that the owner can train or fine-tune with access to the training data. Generative and language models need different designs, and the threshold must reflect the number of classes: an unwatermarked model matched 7.0% of trigger labels on 10-class CIFAR-10 but 1.0% on 100-class CIFAR-100, so chance agreement is far higher with few classes.

resources.title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Deep Neural Networks with Watermarking
resources.abstract: Deep learning technologies, which are the key components of state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI) services, have shown great success in providing human-level capabilities for a variety of tasks, such as visual analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing and etc. Building a production-level deep learning model is a non-trivial task, which requires a large amount of training data, powerful computing resources, and human expertises. Therefore, illegitimate reproducing, distribution, and the derivation of proprietary deep learning models can lead to copyright infringement and economic harm to model creators. Therefore, it is essential to devise a technique to protect the intellectual property of deep learning models and enable external verification of the model ownership. In this paper, we generalize the "digital watermarking'' concept from multimedia ownership verification to deep neural network (DNNs) models. We investigate three DNN-applicable watermark generation algorithms, propose a watermark implanting approach to infuse watermark into deep learning models, and design a remote verification mechanism to determine the model ownership. By extending the intrinsic generalization and memorization capabilities of deep neural networks, we enable the models to learn specially crafted watermarks at training and activate with pre-specified predictions when observing the watermark patterns at inference. We evaluate our approach with two image recognition benchmark datasets. Our framework accurately (100%) and quickly verifies the ownership of all the remotely deployed deep learning models without affecting the model accuracy for normal input data. In addition, the embedded watermarks in DNN models are robust and resilient to different counter-watermark mechanisms, such as fine-tuning, parameter pruning, and model inversion attacks.

resources.title: SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?
resources.abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) watermarking is a method for provenance verification of DNN models. Watermarking should be robust against watermark removal attacks that derive a surrogate model that evades provenance verification. Many watermarking schemes that claim robustness have been proposed, but their robustness is only validated in isolation against a relatively small set of attacks. There is no systematic, empirical evaluation of these claims against a common, comprehensive set of removal attacks. This uncertainty about a watermarking scheme’s robustness causes difficulty to trust their deployment in practice. In this paper, we evaluate whether recently proposed watermarking schemes that claim robustness are robust against a large set of removal attacks. We survey methods from the literature that (i) are known removal attacks, (ii) derive surrogate models but have not been evaluated as removal attacks, and (iii) novel removal attacks. Weight shifting and smooth retraining are novel removal attacks adapted to the DNN watermarking schemes surveyed in this paper. We propose taxonomies for watermarking schemes and removal attacks. Our empirical evaluation includes an ablation study over sets of parameters for each attack and watermarking scheme on the image classification datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Surprisingly, our study shows that none of the surveyed watermarking schemes is robust in practice. We find that schemes fail to withstand adaptive attacks and known methods for deriving surrogate models that have not been evaluated as removal attacks. This points to intrinsic flaws in how robustness is currently evaluated. Our evaluation includes a discussion of the runtime of each attack to underpin their practical relevance. While none of the schemes is robust against all attacks, none of the attacks removes all watermarks. We show that attacks can be combined and find combined attacks that remove all watermarks. We show that watermarking schemes need to be evaluated against a more extensive set of removal attacks with a more realistic adversary model. Our source code and a complete dataset of evaluation results are publicly available, which allows to independently verify our conclusions.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialised in diabetes management to recognise and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.

An insurer's claims-intake assistant is built for routine motor and household claims. Messages about unfamiliar claim types, such as large flood events or commercial losses, are detected and routed to a specialist adjuster instead of being handled with irrelevant questions.

A council's resident-services chatbot covers bin collections, parking permits and council tax. When a resident asks about something it does not cover, such as a planning dispute, it says so, names the service that can help and logs the query, and the log shows the council which topics residents ask about that the chatbot cannot answer.

limitations.description: Scope has to be defined before it can be detected, and general-purpose assistants or fuzzy domains have no clean edge. A narrow definition refuses legitimate queries, and a loose one lets unsupported queries through.

Detection is weakest on queries that resemble in-scope ones. In the 2019 benchmark that introduced the task, no intent classifier caught more than about two-thirds of out-of-scope queries even when trained on examples of them, so recall should be measured on realistic out-of-scope queries before the detector is relied on.
The threshold trades wrongly refusing valid queries against wrongly answering unsupported ones. The two errors rarely cost the same, and queries near the boundary will still land on both sides.
Users can rephrase or disguise an unsupported request so that it resembles in-scope wording. A detector tested only on plain phrasings overstates how well it holds up against paraphrase.

Scope changes as capabilities are added or retired, so the detector and its out-of-scope test set need refreshing, or it will refuse newly supported queries and accept newly unsupported ones. Building realistic out-of-scope examples is costly because annotators need expert knowledge of the in-scope intents.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.

techniques.name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
techniques.description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team evaluating a vendor's sepsis alert scores a year of its own admissions, plots the ROC curve and fixes the alert threshold its operations committee chose from the vendor's recommended range. At that threshold it reports sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and the share of all admissions that would trigger an alert, and uses the false-positive count and alert volume to decide whether ward staff can act on the alerts.

A card-payments company re-runs the analysis every month on transactions its fraud analysts have labelled, confirms that the false-positive rate at the live threshold is still under the limit agreed with its customer-service team, and, whenever the rate has drifted above that limit, reopens the threshold choice on the latest ROC curve and confirms the new threshold on the following month's labelled sample.

A manufacturer's quality engineers choose the threshold for a visual-inspection model by weighing the cost of scrapping a good part against the cost of shipping a defective one, using the ROC curve and the line's defect rate, then report the false-reject and defect-escape rates that the chosen threshold gives on a separate held-out production batch.

A rail operator's safety team assessing a camera-based obstacle detector for level crossings sets the decision threshold on a tuning set so that the miss rate meets the requirement allocated to the detector. It then measures the false-negative rate at that threshold on a separate set of recorded crossings, broken down into daylight, night and rain, and enters the confusion matrices in the safety case as verification evidence.

limitations.description: The rates are evidence only if they are measured on labelled cases that played no part in choosing the threshold. A threshold set to give a 1 per cent false-positive rate on a tuning set gives exactly that rate there by construction, and with a few hundred negative tuning cases its true rate on new data can be half as high again. Choosing the threshold on one set and reporting rates on another, or nesting the choice inside cross-validation, avoids this at the cost of more labelled data.

False-positive and true-positive rates do not change with how common the positive class is, but the share of alerts that are correct does. A false-positive rate within its limit can still mean most alerts are false when the condition is rare: at 90 per cent sensitivity and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, only about 15 per cent of alerts are correct when 1 case in 100 is positive. Claims about alert burden need the positive predictive value at the deployment prevalence as well.

A rate from a finite test set is an estimate, and with few negatives or few errors it can fall well below the true rate by chance. A claim that a rate is within a limit needs a confidence interval (exact binomial for a single rate; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics for other metrics) narrower than the margin to the limit. With no misses, about 3,000 positives show a miss rate below 1 in 1,000, and 30,000 below 1 in 10,000, at 95 per cent confidence.

The threshold is a fixed score, so the rates hold only while the scores for each class stay as in the test set. A new scanner, fraud pattern or patient mix shifts the scores and moves the false-positive rate with no change to the model, so the analysis must be repeated on labelled operational samples, which can be slow or costly. Labels matter too: where only flagged cases are reviewed, the rate for unflagged cases is unknown unless a random sample of them is labelled.

A single rate averages over the whole test set. It can meet its limit overall while exceeding it for a group of people or an operating condition (night-time images, one hospital site) that is rare in the test data. Rates need reporting for each group and condition the claim covers, each with enough cases to be informative, which can multiply the labelled data required.

resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: AutoAttack
techniques.description: AutoAttack is a fixed suite of four automated adversarial attacks, introduced by Croce and Hein (ICML 2020), that measures how much of an image classifier's test accuracy survives small, deliberately chosen changes to its input images at inference time. The evaluator states the threat model, a norm and radius that bound the change (for example, no pixel value changed by more than 8/255 under the L-infinity norm), and the standard version then attacks each correctly classified test image in turn with APGD-CE (projected gradient descent that sets its own step size, on the cross-entropy loss), a targeted APGD on the authors' Difference of Logits Ratio loss, a targeted form of the FAB minimum-norm attack, and the Square Attack, which needs only the model's outputs and so still works when gradients are uninformative. An image counts as robust only if none of the four finds a misclassified version within the bound, and because every attack setting is fixed in advance the evaluator tunes nothing, which removes a common cause of overstated robustness: an attack too weakly tuned for the model. The output is robust accuracy, the share of test images still classified correctly under attack at the stated norm and radius, reported beside clean accuracy; published models are compared on the RobustBench leaderboard, which uses AutoAttack as its standard evaluation. Because AutoAttack is not built around any one defence, it can supply the attack step for a wider judgement of a defence, such as whether adversarial training holds up against attacks it was not trained on; unlike red teaming, it involves no human attacker or open-ended search.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team validating a vendor's classifier that recognises which of 40 identity-document types a customer has photographed during remote account opening, so the right authenticity checks run, receives the model weights under the review agreement. It reruns the vendor's robustness evaluation with standard AutoAttack at the same L-infinity radius, compares the two robust accuracies and records any automatic warnings before accepting the vendor's figure.

A photo-sharing platform's trust-and-safety team expects uploaders to perturb images to slip past the classifier that sorts uploads into a dozen prohibited-content categories and an allowed class. Choosing between two candidate models, it runs standard AutoAttack on both at a perturbation budget agreed with its security team, and selects the one with higher robust accuracy whose clean-accuracy cost is acceptable, recording both figures in the release review.

A research group proposing a new defence for a traffic-sign classifier runs standard AutoAttack before publication and finds that the Square Attack lowers robust accuracy further than the gradient-based attacks, one of AutoAttack's warning signs that gradients are masked. It treats its figure as an upper bound and has an attack designed for its defence built before claiming any robustness.

A computational-pathology group comparing a convolutional network and a vision transformer for three-way tumour subtyping on routine slide images attacks both with AutoAttack, its settings reduced for three classes, at several perturbation sizes below what a blinded clinical reader could detect, and compares attack success rates on an external patient cohort to decide which architecture goes forward.

limitations.description: Robust accuracy from AutoAttack is an upper bound: an image counts as robust because these four attacks failed, not because no adversarial example exists. The authors present it as the minimum test for a new defence rather than the strongest possible attack, so a claim that no change within the bound can alter a decision needs a certified-robustness method instead.

The standard version can overstate robustness for defences that are randomised, not differentiable or run an optimisation loop at inference. The reference code warns about some of these cases, offers a version averaging gradients over the model's randomness, and recommends attacks built for the specific defence; RobustBench excludes such defences. A defence tuned to beat AutoAttack itself can pass it without being robust.

The result holds only for the norm and radius tested. It gives no direct evidence about patches, rotations, physical changes to objects or natural corruptions: in RobustBench's quick-start guide, L-infinity-robust models do much worse than an undefended model on fog-corrupted images, though better on average across corruption types. Benchmark radii such as 8/255 are conventions, so the radius should be justified from the deployment's threat, and a new norm or radius needs a new run.

It needs white-box access: three of the four attacks use the model's gradients, and the code expects raw scores (logits) and inputs scaled to [0, 1]; with access only to output scores, the Square Attack can run alone, a weaker test. The standard settings also assume ten or more classes, since the targeted attacks each try nine other classes; on a binary or few-class model the reference code stops with an error, so the settings must be reduced and the result is no longer the standard one.

The full evaluation is computationally heavy for large models and test sets: each white-box run uses 100 iterations, the targeted attacks each try nine target classes, and the Square Attack makes up to 5,000 queries per image. RobustBench's quick start runs a cheaper two-attack version on 50 images and notes the full version is slower but more accurate; a figure from a subset should be reported with its sampling error.

resources.title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks
resources.abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10\%$, identifying several broken defenses.

techniques.name: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations
techniques.description: Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE) explains one decision of a classifier by generating several altered versions of the input, called counterfactuals, each changed just enough that the model would have given the other outcome, and chosen to differ from one another so that a person sees several distinct ways the result could have been different. Where the contrastive explanation method returns, for one input, a minimal set of features that must be present and a minimal set that must stay absent, DiCE returns several complete alternative inputs at once, within limits the user sets on which features may change and over what range. In the original method all the counterfactuals are optimised together by gradient descent on a loss with three parts: a hinge loss that pushes each across the model's decision threshold, a distance term (each continuous feature's change divided by its median absolute deviation in the training data, plus the share of categorical features changed) that keeps each close to the original, and a diversity term, the determinant of a similarity matrix between them, that rewards them for differing. Afterwards, small changes are reset to their original values for as long as the counterfactual still gets the other outcome, to make it sparser, and counterfactuals that break causal rules supplied by the user, such as gaining a degree without growing older, can be filtered out. The method as published needs a differentiable model such as a neural network; the reference library adds random-sampling, genetic-algorithm and nearest-training-example searches that need only the model's predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A credit-risk validation team at a lender generates five counterfactuals for each of 500 sampled refused applications with every feature free to change, to see what the model treats as enough for approval. Counterfactuals that reach approval by changing only the postcode, or another likely proxy for a protected characteristic, are logged as findings and passed to the fairness testing team.

A hospital team piloting a classifier that places patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in low, moderate or high cardiovascular risk generates counterfactuals restricted to modifiable factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking. Clinicians check whether the changes the model links to a lower risk category agree with clinical knowledge before the tool is shown to patients.

A consumer lender puts up to three counterfactuals in each refusal letter, generated against the model version that made the decision and limited to features the applicant can change (income, balances, loan amount and term), each shown as an application that would have been approved. Before rollout it tests a draft letter with applicants, checking that they can name a change that would have worked and understand that the options are not a promise of approval if they reapply.

limitations.description: A counterfactual is only valid for the model version that produced it. The method assumes the model does not change, and after retraining a previously suggested change can stop flipping the decision, so a person who acts on it may still be refused. Counterfactuals shown to people should be dated, tied to a model version and re-checked whenever the model is updated.

Feasibility depends on constraints the user supplies. Without them, counterfactuals can change attributes a person cannot change, such as race or sex, or propose impossible combinations: in the original experiments over a third of the counterfactuals that changed education were infeasible, most raising the degree without raising age. Causal rules can only be applied afterwards, as a filter.

The set returned is not unique. It depends on the weights on distance and diversity, per-feature weights, the number requested and random starting points, and with the library's random-sampling method a different seed gives a different set. The authors note that showing people counterfactuals produced with different settings is a problem, so fix and record settings and seeds.

Distance is measured feature by feature (scaled change for numbers, changed or not for categories), so it ignores how features move together, treats every category change as equally hard, and can place counterfactuals where there is little real data. In a study of 9,613 patient records, DiCE's counterfactuals were closer and sparser but less plausible than those of a sampling-based alternative.

The original paper tests no people. Its stand-in for understanding, a nearest-neighbour model trained on the counterfactuals, is in the authors' words a best case of rational extrapolation, and they leave a behavioural study and the cost of choosing among more options to future work. A counterfactual also does not say which features must stay as they are, so a person who raises income by changing job may still be refused. Test the wording with recipients before relying on it.

techniques.name: Predictive Parity and Calibration Within Groups
techniques.description: This test checks whether a model's output means the same for every group: among people who receive the same score or the same decision, the share who turn out to have the outcome (or its average, for an outcome such as a cost or a count of illnesses) should not depend on their group, a requirement the fairness literature calls sufficiency. For a model that outputs a risk score, cases with known outcomes are grouped into score bins and, for each group, the observed outcome rate in each bin is plotted against the score, giving one calibration curve per group (a score is calibrated when, of the cases scored 0.3, about 30 per cent have the outcome); calibration within groups (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan) holds when each group's curve matches the scores, and the weaker condition that the curves coincide holds when a given score corresponds to the same outcome rate in every group. For a yes/no decision the same comparison is made in the two cells of the decision: predictive parity (Chouldechova) holds when the positive predictive value, the share of people flagged positive who turn out positive, is equal across groups, and the negative predictive value can be compared in the same way for those not flagged. The two read-outs can disagree, because a score that means the same for every group can still give unequal positive predictive values at a threshold when the groups' scores are spread differently above it, so the test reports the read-out matching the output on which decisions are taken, with intervals and the gaps between groups. Where comparisons of error rates condition on the true outcome and ask whether people who turn out the same are treated the same, this test conditions on the model's output and asks whether people treated the same turn out the same; when the outcome is more common in one group, the two cannot both hold except in special cases.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team checks a deterioration-risk score before it is shown to ward staff. On a year of admissions with recorded outcomes it plots a calibration curve, with intervals, for each ethnic group and each sex, and approves the score for use with every patient only if, across the scores that trigger escalation, each group's curve stays within a band agreed with clinicians.

A lender's model validation team compares the repayment rate among approved applicants across age bands, using two years of outcomes, to check whether approval means the same for each band. Because a difference among the approved can come from how scores are spread above the cut-off rather than from a different bar for one band, it also compares the calibration curves of the underlying score before raising any finding with the credit risk committee.

A probation service assessing a supplier's reoffending-risk tool is shown evidence that its positive predictive value is equal across ethnic groups. Its analysts reproduce the figures on local data and set them beside the groups' false positive and false negative rates, which differ because reconviction rates differ, so that the oversight board chooses which criterion the tool will be held to with both sets of figures in front of it.

A health insurer auditing a score that selects members for a care-management programme checks twice whether the score means the same for every racial group: against next year's costs, the label the model was trained on, and against a measure of illness such as the number of active chronic conditions. A score calibrated for cost but not for illness, with one group sicker than another at the same score, would lead the insurer to retrain on a different label.

limitations.description: When the outcome is more common in one group, a score or decision that satisfies predictive parity cannot also give the groups both equal false positive and equal false negative rates, and calibration within groups cannot coexist with equal average scores for each group's positives and negatives except with perfect prediction or equal base rates (Chouldechova; Kleinberg et al.). Passing this test therefore means accepting unequal error rates, a choice the test informs but cannot make.

Passing says little about how accurately the model predicts for each group. A well-fitted model usually comes close to calibration within groups without any fairness intervention when group membership can be inferred from its inputs, and a model that predicts accurately for one group while giving everyone in another group that group's average rate is still perfectly calibrated (Barocas, Hardt and Narayanan). The result needs pairing with performance measured for each group.

The test uses recorded outcomes, so it inherits any difference between groups in how the outcome is recorded. Rearrest stands in for reoffending, and a care-management score was calibrated by race for health costs while, at the 97th percentile of the score, Black patients had 26 per cent more chronic illnesses than white patients (Obermeyer et al.). A model can pass while scoring one group's need too low, so the outcome tested must be the one the claim is about.

A gap in positive predictive value is not by itself evidence that the score treats groups differently: the value averages over everyone above the threshold, so it depends on how each group's scores are spread there and moves when the threshold moves. Chouldechova notes that well-calibrated scores can fail predictive parity, and the converse also holds. Where scores are available the calibration curves should be reported, and the threshold stated.

Per-group calibration curves need labelled cases across the score range in every group; in a small group the high-score bins may hold a handful of people, so their rates swing widely, and the choice of bin widths changes the picture. An outside auditor who sees only decisions, not scores, can test predictive parity but not calibration, so access determines which claim the evidence can support.

resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

sample_claims.text: Across the deterioration-risk scores that trigger escalation, each ethnic group's observed deterioration rate lies within 3 percentage points of the rate for all patients with the same score, with the 95 per cent interval for each gap inside that band, on twelve months of admissions held out from model development.

Among applicants approved by the credit model in the evaluation period, the repayment rate for each age band is within 2 percentage points of the rate for all approved applicants, and the calibration curves of the underlying score for each band are reported alongside.

At the deployed threshold, the reoffending-risk tool's positive predictive value differs between ethnic groups by less than 5 percentage points on local data, and the corresponding differences in false positive and false negative rates are reported with it.

At each decile of the care-management score, the mean number of active chronic conditions differs between racial groups by less than the tolerance agreed with the clinical lead, so the score indicates the same level of illness in every group, not only the same expected cost.

techniques.name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
techniques.description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team validating a credit-risk model before release audits its decisions on a held-out sample of past applicants whose repayment is known, and records that these are only applicants the old policy approved. It searches subgroups over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status for the worst false positive rate gap (good payers flagged as high risk), compares it with a limit agreed with the risk committee, and sends the rule for any subgroup over it to the developers.

A hospital's clinical AI team has confirmed that a sepsis early-warning model misses cases at similar rates for men and women and for each recorded ethnic group. Before rollout it audits the false negative rate over subgroups combining age, sex and ethnicity and, because the search is approximate, also scores a grid of rules over two of the attributes by brute force, as the method's authors did, to check the search did not miss a larger gap.

A local authority's internal audit team re-audits a model that flags housing benefit claims for fraud review each quarter, using a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged. It records the worst subgroup by false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged) over age, sex, ethnicity and disability, with its size and gap, and escalates to the system owner when the weighted gap exceeds the agreed limit.

limitations.description: Finding the worst subgroup exactly is hard in the worst case, even for conjunctions or linear thresholds of attributes (Kearns et al. 2018, Theorem 3.3), so practical audits use a heuristic search. A subgroup it reports does have the measured gap on the audit data, but a clean result is only a lower bound: the authors note their auditor could miss a larger disparity and checked it by brute force on two attributes (Kearns et al. 2019). 'Nothing found' is a search result, not a proof.

Gaps are weighted by subgroup size, which the authors require for reliable estimates and which lets small groups pass with large gaps: a subgroup holding 2% of the records whose false positive rate is 20 percentage points above the overall rate scores at most 0.004, under the 0.005 limit used in the AIF360 demonstration. The audit cannot support a claim about a small named group; report that group's own rate, with an interval, instead.

Only subgroups that the rule class can describe, over the attributes designated as protected, are searched; the reference implementation uses linear threshold rules. The class has to be limited because, as the authors note, any imperfect classifier could be accused of unfairness to the set of people it misclassifies. A protected attribute that is not recorded or not designated is invisible, so the attributes used and their encoding must be stated with the finding.

Error-rate audits need the protected attributes and the true outcome for every audited record, which a deployed system may not supply, for example when outcomes are seen only for approved applications. Reliable estimates need more data the richer the subgroup class, the authors' experiments report in-sample results, and the tools give no confidence interval, so audit on held-out data and repeat on fresh data before relying on a worst-case figure.

It tests parity of one rate at a time for binary decisions, each subgroup's rate against the overall rate. A pass on false positives says nothing about false negatives, the AIF360 auditor implements only those two error rates, and other criteria, such as whether scores mean the same in every subgroup (calibration), need a different test. The rate must be chosen to match the fairness claim before the audit.

resources.title: Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness
resources.abstract: The most prevalent notions of fairness in machine learning fix a small collection of pre-defined groups (such as race or gender), and then ask for approximate parity of some statistic of the classifier (such as false positive rate) across these groups. Constraints of this form are susceptible to fairness gerrymandering, in which a classifier is fair on each individual group, but badly violates the fairness constraint on structured subgroups, such as certain combinations of protected attribute values. We thus consider fairness across exponentially or infinitely many subgroups, defined by a structured class of functions over the protected attributes. We first prove that the problem of auditing subgroup fairness for both equality of false positive rates and statistical parity is computationally equivalent to the problem of weak agnostic learning — which means it is hard in the worst case, even for simple structured subclasses. However, it also suggests that common heuristics for learning can be applied to successfully solve the auditing problem in practice. We then derive an algorithm that provably converges in a polynomial number of steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers, given access to an oracle which can solve the agnostic learning problem. The algorithm is based on a formulation of subgroup fairness as a zero-sum game between a Learner (the primal player) and an Auditor (the dual player). We implement a variant of this algorithm using heuristic oracles, and show that we can effectively both audit and learn fair classifiers on a real dataset.
